title: FCC Fines Eight Suspected DJI Front Companies and Moves to Ban Military-Grade Drone Imports
excerpt: The agency proposed $25,000 penalties against firms allegedly selling rebranded DJI hardware while ignoring federal inquiries, and tentatively decided to prohibit imports of swarming and infrared-equipped drones.
body:
• The FCC proposed $25,000 fines against eight companies it suspects of selling rebranded DJI drones and cameras in the U.S. under different brand names.
  • None of the eight firms responded to FCC Letters of Inquiry issued in May, prompting enforcement action with a July 20 deadline.
  • Separately, the FCC tentatively decided to ban imports of foreign-made military-grade drones, including swarming drones and those with infrared technology.
  • DJI, which holds over half the U.S. commercial drone market, is challenging its Covered List placement in a Ninth Circuit lawsuit.

FCC Targets Alleged Shell Companies

The Federal Communications Commission on July 10 proposed $25,000 fines against eight companies it suspects of funneling DJI technology into the United States under alternative brand names. The companies — Cogito Tech, Fikaxo Technology, Lyno Dynamics, Skyhigh Tech, Spatial Hover, SZ Knowact Robot, WaveGo Tech, and Xtra Technology — all failed to respond to Letters of Inquiry the FCC's Enforcement Bureau sent in May 2026.

The inquiries asked whether each company had "indirectly or directly marketed within the United States any radiofrequency equipment" on the FCC's Covered List. The base forfeiture for ignoring FCC communications is $4,000, but the Bureau raised each penalty to $25,000, calling the conduct "egregious, intentional, and continuous."

Several companies have drawn scrutiny for products mirroring DJI hardware. SZ Knowact is behind the Skyrover drone brand, whose lineup tracks DJI's catalog model for model. Xtra Technology sells action cameras resembling DJI's Osmo Action series. Security researcher Konrad Iturbe documented the connections months earlier using automated protocol scans that flagged DJI's proprietary communication signatures in the companies' FCC filings.

Military-Grade Drone Import Ban Proposed

In a separate move on July 21, the FCC tentatively decided to ban imports of foreign-produced military-grade drones, including swarming drones and those with infrared technology, according to Reuters. The agency said swarm-enabled drones "can overwhelm defenses, provide persistent surveillance, and create complex operational challenges that strain traditional air defense systems."

"The paper trail has caught up with all eight. The shell-company pipeline was an open secret that most of the mainstream press would not touch."

— DroneXL, which first reported on the suspected front companies in September 2025

The proposed order would not cover drones purchased by the federal government or non-military-grade equipment. Existing exemptions for non-Chinese drone components will be extended until January 2028. A 30-day public comment period precedes any final decision.

The Broader Crackdown on Chinese Drone Tech

Both actions extend the FCC's escalating campaign against Chinese drone technology. In December 2025, the agency added foreign-made drones to its Covered List, barring DJI, Autel Robotics, and other Chinese manufacturers from obtaining FCC approval for new U.S. products. DJI was added not because the government found specific security flaws, but because no federal agency completed the security audit Congress mandated under the FY2025 NDAA before the December 23 deadline.

The FCC also granted itself power to retroactively revoke previously approved equipment authorizations — a tool directly relevant to the current crackdown. If investigations confirm the eight fined companies are selling DJI hardware in disguise, their existing authorizations can be pulled.

DJI Fights Back in Court

DJI filed a lawsuit in the Ninth Circuit in February 2026, arguing the FCC's decision had "serious procedural flaws" and that the agency "never identified any threat associated with DJI or its products." The company claims the ban will cost it $1.56 billion in 2026 alone.

"firm OnDefend, published in May, found no critical security issues in tested DJI products, no evidence of data leaving the United States, and no backdoors."

An independent audit by U.S. firm OnDefend, published in May, found no critical security issues in tested DJI products, no evidence of data leaving the United States, and no backdoors. In June, the FCC partially retreated by exempting Chinese toy drones after the Pentagon determined they lacked the capabilities to pose a national security risk.

What Comes Next

The July 20 response deadline for the eight companies has passed. If they remain silent, the FCC is expected to pursue revoking their equipment authorizations. The military-grade drone ban enters a 30-day comment period. DJI's Ninth Circuit case could reshape the landscape — a ruling narrowing the Covered List designation would undermine the legal basis for every enforcement action since December. For Indian-Americans who rely on DJI products for photography or commercial work, purchased drones remain legal to fly, but future app updates, firmware support, and replacement parts may become harder to access.
image_caption: A DJI Mavic Pro drone displayed against a white background. The Chinese manufacturer faces escalating U.S. regulatory action including fines against suspected front companies and proposed bans on military-grade drone imports.
nri_angle: Indian-American drone users and NRI photographers relying on DJI equipment face uncertainty over future firmware support, app availability, and parts access as the U.S. crackdown intensifies.
